newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Fraud hits Philippine cellular companies.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fraud hits Philippine cellular companies.

text.p: The lucrative Philippine mobile phone industry is being plagued by fraud, prompting players to adopt expensive counter-measures and seek tough new legislation to help stem the problem.
National Telecommunications Commission head Simeon Kintanar told Reuters the entire industry was suffering from fraud.
"From what I hear from the players, they are being hit by two types of fraud, namely subscriber fraud and cloning," he said.
Pilipino Telephone Corp, the cellular firm with the biggest subscriber base of nearly 400,000, said that in 1996 alone it expected to lose 300 million pesos in revenue from cloning.
In this type of fraud, a phone number is copied and the charges dumped on the legitimate holder of that number.

"Cloners took advantage of our switch last April to a digital narrow-band advanced mobile phone system, defrauding the company of millions of pesos," said Ignatius Yenko, Piltel chief financial officer.
Yenko said that before the switch to the new system, the company was being defrauded of eight to 10 million pesos a month through cloning. This figure more than doubled after the switch.
"With cloning, simultaneous calls were made on one number because when we did the switch-over, the software that would prevent simultaneous calls from happening was absent," he said.

Another mobile phone company, Globe Telecom GMCR Inc, was a victim of subscription fraud. It said it had to set aside 441 million pesos in the second quarter of 1996 to compensate for doubtful accounts.

The company, owned by Ayala Corp and Singapore Telecom, was the first to publicly admit that fraud was eating into its revenues. It reported a net loss of 466.951 million pesos for the first six months of the year.

"There were internal lapses in our credit system, allowing a syndicate to use papers of qualified individuals to avail of our phones. There were also multiple applications," Globe Telecom president Filemon Berba said.

Berba said that to prevent a recurrence, Globe overhauled its system, installing new software and hardware to keep better track of accounts, re-training support staff and enhancing its after-sales monitoring.

The fraud also made Globe more careful about taking on new subscribers. "We have restrained our people from just getting any customer. We want good-quality subscribers," said Cesar Sison, Globe Telecom senior consultant.

Piltel said it is spending $10 million on anti-fraud software and hardware. The anti-fraud measures include enhancing Piltel's capacity to store personal identification numbers and a system that records a subscriber's calling pattern so that any deviation will automatically alert the company.

Yenko said expensive technology called "phone printing" will allow Piltel to stop calls from cloned cellular phones. The technology, to be adopted next year, identifies the unique frequency characteristics of every cell phone so that a call from a cloned phone will not get through.
The company hopes these measures will bring Piltel's loses down to five million pesos a month from next year, Yenko said.
Officials of Smart Communications Co Inc declined to discuss specific details about fraud, saying it could adversely affect Smart's plans for an initial public share offering.

Without giving details, its parent, Metro Pacific Corp, said Smart has been able to avoid problems with cloning through sophisticated software and technical controls. Smart also carefully screened new accounts to reduce instances of fraud, Metro Pacific said in a statement.
The two other cellular operators, Isla Communications Co Inc (Islacom) and Express Telecommunications Philippines Inc (Extelcom) have not reported any major cases of fraud.
Piltel president Ramon Cojuangco said in an interview that the government would have to help tackle the fraud problem.
"We need an anti-fraud law that will impose stiffer penalties so that mere possession of a cloned phone is enough to send one to jail," Cojuangco said.

The Department of Transportation and Communications and the telecommunications commission support new laws but Kintanar said cell phone companies should also band together to develop a joint database on fraudulent subscribers.
"Fraud is a continuous activity. We cannot eliminate it but we can manage it," Sison, of Globe Telecom, said.
